Caplan writes:
>Samuel Knoche, a student at Fordham University, has taken me up on an old bet:

---

>I bet at even odds that 10 years from now, the fraction of American 18-24 year-olds enrolled in traditional four-year colleges will be no more than 10% (not 10 percentage-points!) lower than it is today.

---

However, we’ve slightly modified the earlier terms.
> Since the most recent data is for 2015, we are betting that when the 2025 data comes out, Samuel [Knoche] wins if the fraction of 18-to-24-years-olds enrolled in four-year colleges has fallen more than 10%.  I win if it’s fallen less.  Since the current rate is 29.9%, he wins if the rate is 26.6% or less.  If the data series is discontinued, we call off the bet and I refund his money with 3% annual interest.

---

**Should College Come With a Money-Back Guarantee?**
The U.S. Department of Education has proposed new rules allowing students to sue universities for tuition reimbursement if the institution substantially misrepresents key aspects of education, such as graduate employability or program content. Unlike traditional fraud law (mens rea), which requires proof of intent, this new standard permits lawsuits even if the misrepresentation was unintentional—such as a clerical error. This could expose universities, including public institutions like the University of Colorado at Boulder, to liability, potentially requiring taxpayer funding for refunds. The proposal arises amid concerns over rising student debt—$1.2 trillion in 2015—and low graduation rates, with less than 20% of full-time students at public four-year colleges earning degrees within four years. The article draws a parallel between education and consumer goods: just as consumers can return defective products like cars, TVs, or spoiled milk for refunds, students might reasonably expect a similar recourse if their degree fails to deliver promised outcomes, such as job placement in their field. The central question posed is whether college should come with a money-back guarantee, reflecting a broader debate about accountability, value, and consumer protection in higher education.

Experts across higher education policy, demographics, economics, sociology, and education studies broadly converge that Bryan Caplan's chances of winning his bet—that the 18-24 year-old four-year college enrollment rate in 2025 will be greater than 26.6%—have become significantly less likely due to a confluence of negative shocks in 2025. All experts cite a historically unprecedented 17% drop in new international student enrollment, primarily due to catastrophic US visa processing failures, building on a 7% decline the previous year. This loss disproportionately affects four-year institutions, as international students make up a significant share of their enrollment.

Domestic headwinds are also substantial: the US is experiencing a demographic 'enrollment cliff' of declining high school graduates (shrinking the pool of new entrants), deepening public skepticism about the value of a college degree, and stagnant or declining real federal financial aid. Colleges are responding with unprecedented admissions flexibility (waivers, direct admissions, extended deadlines), aggressive outreach, and increased financial aid, which most experts assess as slightly blunting but not reversing the declines in both international and domestic enrollment. Some also highlight that the base rate for such a sharp enrollment drop (more than 10% in a decade) is low, which could buffer the impact.

The modal expert expectation is that the 2025 NCES four-year college enrollment rate for 18-24-year-olds will be very close to the 26.6% threshold, with a somewhat higher chance that it will fall to or just below this line (meaning Caplan loses the bet), but with notable uncertainty and plausible narrow win scenarios. Most assign probabilities for a Caplan win in the 20-45% range, with a minority slightly higher (62-63%) based on historical inertia and institutional adaptability, and the lowest at 20-25% for those weighing the international student collapse most heavily. Reasoning is largely consistent: negative shocks this year are sharper than any since the COVID-19 pandemic or, in some accounts, since the 1970s, but so is institutional motivation to prevent a steep decline. In sum, the expert consensus anticipates a high risk of Caplan losing, but with a real (albeit minority) probability that resilient institutional responses and the structural stickiness of enrollment rates keep the figure just above the threshold.
